title: lncRNA HOTAIR promotes airway remodeling by regulating metabolic reprogramming through the FUS/HK2 axis in airway smooth muscle cells.
abstract: Airway remodeling is a critical pathological feature of chronic airway diseases and is closely associated with irreversible airflow limitation. Increasing evidence indicates that metabolic reprogramming contributes to airway smooth muscle cell (ASMC) remodeling; however, the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Human ASMCs were stimulated with platelet-derived growth factor-BB (PDGF-BB) to establish an in vitro remodeling model. HOTAIR expression was manipulated using siRNA-mediated knockdown, while FUS and HK2 were restored by plasmid overexpression. Cell viability, proliferation, migration, glycolytic metabolism, and remodeling-associated protein expression were assessed using CCK-8, EdU staining, Transwell assays, Seahorse extracellular flux analysis, qRT-PCR, and western blotting. RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) and mRNA stability assays were performed to investigate the interaction among HOTAIR, FUS, and HK2. HOTAIR expression was significantly upregulated in PDGF-BB-stimulated ASMCs. HOTAIR knockdown markedly inhibited ASMC proliferation, migration, and ECM remodeling, with reduced expression of Collagen I, Fibronectin, MMP9, and α-SMA. HOTAIR silencing suppressed glucose uptake, lactate production, ATP generation, and ECAR while partially restoring mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. FUS directly bound both HOTAIR and HK2 mRNA; HOTAIR depletion accelerated HK2 mRNA degradation, whereas FUS restoration rescued HK2 mRNA stability. Re-expression of either FUS or HK2 reversed the inhibitory effects of HOTAIR silencing on glycolytic metabolism and ASMC remodeling phenotypes. HOTAIR promotes PDGF-BB-induced glycolytic reprogramming and airway smooth muscle remodeling by stabilizing HK2 mRNA through the RNA-binding protein FUS. T These findings suggest that the HOTAIR/FUS/HK2 axis contributes to PDGF-BB-induced ASMC remodeling and may represent a potential therapeutic target.

title: Targeting protein arginine methyltransferases to enhance cancer immunotherapy.
abstract: Arginine methylation is a post-translational modification found on many proteins, including RNA-binding proteins, signaling molecules, histones, and heat shock proteins, where it can alter protein-protein and protein-nucleic acid interactions. Arginine methylation regulates many cellular pathways, including RNA metabolism, signal transduction, gene expression, cellular stress responses, DNA repair, and, more recently, innate immune sensing. Here, we discuss recent advances in innate immune sensing and the emerging role of arginine methylation in suppressing tumor immune visibility. We describe current knowledge of protein arginine methyltransferase (PRMT) inhibitors and degraders and their use from preclinical models to clinical trials, alone or in combination with other therapies, to reduce tumor progression and enhance the effectiveness of cancer immunotherapy.

title: Protein arginine methylation rewires molecular interactions.
abstract: Protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMT1-9) catalyze monomethylation and dimethylation of arginine residues in RNA- and DNA-associated proteins. Protein arginine methylation can weaken or strengthen nucleic acid binding, recruit or exclude protein partners, and promote or suppress higher-order assembly, making its molecular consequences highly context dependent. Methylation preserves the cationic character of the guanidinium group, while altering hydrogen-bond donor topology, steric accessibility, and interaction geometry. These effects are particularly consequential in intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), where arginine-rich motifs mediate multivalent protein-protein and protein-nucleic acid interactions. Here, we propose an interaction-equilibrium framework in which arginine methylation redistributes binding capacity among the competing protein, nucleic acid, and assembly states. This framework integrates reader-dependent and reader-independent effects of methylarginine and provides a chemical basis for understanding how a charge-preserving modification can reweight molecular interactions across diverse cellular contexts.

title: A promoter G-quadruplex recruits Hrb27C to regulate NEMO and immune defense against Lyme disease pathogens in the deer tick.
abstract: Genomic DNA can adopt noncanonical secondary structures, such as G-quadruplexes (G4s), which serve as critical regulatory elements beyond the traditional double helix. Whether promoter G4s also participate in controlling innate immune signaling and host-pathogen interactions, however, remains unknown in arthropods. In this study, we identify a G4 structure within the promoter of the NEMO (NF-κB essential modulator) gene in the deer tick Ixodes scapularis. Using a combination of circular dichroism, isothermal difference spectra, and fluorescence-based assays, we demonstrate that this sequence forms a stable, parallel G4 topology in vitro and in vivo. Functional characterization via luciferase reporter assays reveals that this G4 scaffold is essential for proper NEMO transcriptional output. Importantly, disruption of the G4 structure significantly reduces NEMO expression and increases the burden of the Lyme disease spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. Genome-wide expression profiling further reveals that perturbation of the NEMO G4 produces transcriptional changes that overlap with those observed following NEMO silencing. These shared transcriptional responses are enriched for immune-associated genes and ribonucleoprotein-related pathways. We further identify the heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein Hrb27C as a structural binding protein that specifically recognizes the NEMO G4 through its RNA recognition motif domains and facilitates NEMO expression. Collectively, our findings establish promoter G4 architecture as an important regulatory layer in tick immunity, linking DNA topology to pathogen proliferation and providing a structural framework for understanding host-pathogen dynamics in disease vectors.

title: Genome-Wide Characterization of the Wheat Pum Gene Family and Heterologous Functional Analysis of TaPum-III-5b in Arabidopsis Under Salt Stress.
abstract: Pumilio (Pum)-family proteins are evolutionarily conserved RNA-binding proteins that regulate post-transcriptional processes; however, their specific functions in staple crops, for example, wheat (Triticum aestivum), remain poorly understood. We identified 56 TaPum genes and classified them into three phylogenetic subgroups (I-III). The larger TaPum family size in allohexaploid wheat was associated with retention of A-, B-, and D-subgenome homoeologs, segmental duplication, and tandem duplication. After separating homoeologous pairs, 17 segmental duplication pairs and five tandem duplication pairs were identified, and ratios of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitutions (Ka/Ks) below 1 were consistent with purifying selection. Subgroup-specific motifs and the uneven distribution of cis-acting elements, particularly abscisic acid (ABA)- and methyl jasmonate (MeJA)-responsive elements, suggested potential divergence in promoter regulatory architecture. Transcriptomic profiling and independent quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction analysis showed more consistent response of TaPum genes to salt stress than to cold or drought stress. Salt stress strongly promoted TaPum-III-5b expression, and its encoded protein exhibited nuclear and cytoplasmic localization. Heterologous overexpression of TaPum-III-5b in Arabidopsis thaliana increased salt tolerance, as indicated by enhanced survival; augmented peroxidase, superoxide dismutase, and catalase activities; and diminished accumulation of reactive oxygen species and malondialdehyde. Electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) demonstrated sequence-specific binding of TaDREB2B to a dehydration-responsive element (DRE)-containing sequence in the TaPum-III-5b promoter, whereas dual-luciferase (Dual-LUC) analysis showed activation of the wild-type promoter. Together, these results support a proposed regulatory framework in which TaPum-III-5b may contribute to salt-stress responses through as-yet-unidentified downstream RNA targets. This study characterizes the Pum gene family in wheat and identifies the TaDREB2B-TaPum-III-5b module as a candidate regulatory pathway associated with salt-stress responses. Its potential application in wheat improvement requires further validation in wheat.

title: Cross-domain signal grammars of transcription termination.
abstract: Transcription termination establishes gene boundaries, recycles RNA polymerase, and prevents interference between neighboring transcription units. Termination depends on cis-acting elements, trans-acting factors, and the susceptibility of the elongation complex to pausing, cleavage, destabilization, or release. Predicted motifs, stable RNA ends, processing sites, readthrough regions, and polymerase-release regions are nevertheless often treated as measurements of the same event, which complicates mechanistic comparison and model development. This review compares termination signals as context-dependent rule systems in which sequence determinants, RNA structure and accessibility, and processing sites are interpreted through their order and spacing, molecular readers, conditional gates, and kinetic windows. It examines bacterial intrinsic and Rho-dependent termination, archaeal U-rich and cleavage-linked routes, PAS-centered RNAPII termination, and nuclear Pol I, Pol III, and specialized RNAPII pathways, showing how shared kinetic constraints are met by divergent molecular solutions shaped by cellular organization. Matching each signal feature to the measurement that supports it clarifies cross-domain comparisons and guides transcriptome-wide analysis, prediction, and terminator engineering in defined biological systems.

title: HOXA3 Knockdown Impairs hESC-Derived Thymic Epithelial-like Cell Differentiation and CXCL12-Associated Early T-Lineage Support.
abstract: Thymic epithelial cells (TECs) provide essential signals for T-cell development, yet the mechanisms governing human TEC differentiation and the acquisition of T-cell-supporting function remain incompletely understood. Using a three-stage system that directs human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) through definitive endoderm and third pharyngeal pouch endoderm (3PPE) toward a thymic epithelial-like lineage, we investigated the role of HOXA3 during thymic epithelial-like cell (TEC-like cell) differentiation. HOXA3 knockdown during 3PPE-to-TEC-like cell transition impaired thymic epithelial differentiation, as indicated by reduced K8, AIRE, and CD205 expression and decreased FOXN1 protein. HOXA3-knockdown TEC-like cells also showed a markedly reduced capacity to support the generation of CD45+CD3+ cells from cord blood CD34+ progenitors. Bulk RNA sequencing identified 1040 upregulated and 774 downregulated genes, revealing broad remodeling of cell-cycle, motility, chemotaxis, angiogenesis, and tissue-remodeling programs. CXCL12 was among the downregulated genes, and its reduction was confirmed at both mRNA and protein levels. Motif analysis identified a putative HOXA3-binding site, and conventional ChIP-PCR showed enrichment of the predicted CXCL12 regulatory region in HOXA3 immunoprecipitates. Recombinant CXCL12 significantly increased CD45+CD3+ cell generation in HOXA3-knockdown co-cultures. Together, these data support an association between HOXA3 knockdown, reduced acquisition of a thymic epithelial-like phenotype, and diminished early T-lineage support, with CXCL12 partially accounting for the functional phenotype. This study provides a tractable hESC-based model for studying human thymic epithelial development and TEC-mediated early T-lineage differentiation.

title: Genetic and Epigenetic Manipulation Using CRISPR Techniques in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: CRISPR-based technologies have transformed experimental biology by enabling precise, efficient, and programmable manipulation of the genome and epigenome. This chapter provides a comprehensive and practical guide to genetic and epigenetic editing using CRISPR technology, with a particular focus on applications in Ewing sarcoma cell models. We describe strategies for CRISPR-mediated gene knockout (CRISPR KO) via nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ), precise gene knock-in (CRISPR KI) through homology-directed repair (HDR), and reversible transcriptional modulation using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) and CRISPR activation (CRISPRa). We emphasize the use of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery of Cas9 and single guide RNAs, which offers improved editing efficiency, reduced off-target activity, and enhanced safety compared to plasmid-based approaches. Detailed protocols are provided for guide RNA design, RNP assembly, electroporation-based delivery, single-cell cloning, and molecular validation of edited clones. In addition, we outline best practices for HDR template design, discuss strategies to improve KI efficiency, and address common challenges such as polyploidy, variable editing rates, and DNA-mediated cytotoxicity. For CRISPRi and CRISPRa applications, we describe plasmid-based systems employing catalytically inactive Cas9 fused to transcriptional repressors or activators, enabling potentially tunable and reversible control of endogenous gene expression. Throughout the chapter, practical advice, troubleshooting tips, and critical considerations are included to facilitate successful implementation across diverse experimental settings. Collectively, this chapter serves as a detailed methodological resource for researchers aiming to employ CRISPR-based engineering for functional studies.

title: Methyltransferase RsmB chaperones E. coli ribosome assembly by orchestrating the recruitment of ribosomal proteins.
abstract: Ribosomal RNA modification enzymes increase cellular fitness, but it's little known whether this benefit arises from rRNA modification or a chaperone function of the modification enzyme. Here, we show that E. coli methyltransferase RsmB chaperones the initial recruitment of ribosomal proteins to the 16S 3' domain rRNA, a key step in assembly of the 30S subunit. Real-time single-molecule assembly experiments show that the RsmB product, 16S m5C967, has little effect on the rRNA affinity for ribosomal proteins. Instead, RsmB facilitates stable recruitment of primary protein uS7 during transcription while blocking the addition of secondary protein uS19. Completion of the methyltransferase cycle promotes RsmB release, allowing assembly to continue. Dimethyl sulfate footprinting of trapped RsmB-rRNA complexes revealed that RsmB restructures a critical rRNA helix junction. Our results illustrate how an RNA modification enzyme favors the proper sequence of protein addition by temporarily reshaping the energy landscape of co-transcriptional rRNA folding.

title: Complete genome sequencing and molecular characterization of Jasminum polyanthum rubodvirus 1, a virus representative of a putative novel species in the genus Rubodvirus.
abstract: To identify viruses infecting Jasminum polyanthum (pink jasmine), symptomatic leaves were collected from Yunnan Province, China, and subjected to virus detection and molecular characterization. A virus was identified and tentatively named Jasminum polyanthum rubodvirus 1 (JPRV1). The virus belongs to the genus Rubodvirus within the family Phenuiviridae (order Hareavirales). The genome of JPRV1 consists of three negative-sense single-stranded RNA segments: RNA1 (7,204 nt), RNA2 (1,492 nt), and RNA3 (1,466 nt), encoding the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp; L protein), movement protein (MP), and nucleocapsid protein (N), respectively. Sequence comparisons showed that the JPRV1 L protein shared 37.46%-42.87% amino acid sequence identity with those of recognized Rubodvirus species. Phylogenetic analysis placed JPRV1 in a distinct lineage within the genus Rubodvirus. These findings support the classification of JPRV1 as a virus representative of a putative novel species in the genus Rubodvirus and provide the first report of a rubodvirus associated with J. polyanthum.

title: Optimisation and mechanistic characterization of a selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor in pancreatic cancer cells.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a lethal malignancy with limited targeted therapeutic options. Mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase kinase 4 (MAP4K4) has been implicated in PDAC progression, but the development of effective MAP4K4 inhibitors requires further improvement in potency, selectivity, and mechanistic characterisation. We previously identified F389-0746 as a selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor with anti-cancer activity in pancreatic cancer. Here, we used the F389-0746 scaffold to guide the selection and evaluation of benzoxazine-based analogs, followed by biochemical, structural, selectivity, and cellular characterisation of the most potent analogue. Among the identified analogs, F389-0736 showed the strongest MAP4K4 inhibitory activity, with an IC50 value of 44.0 nM, representing an approximately threefold improvement over F389-0746. Docking and structure-activity relationship analyses identified key binding interactions that support the enhanced potency of F389-0736 within the MAP4K4 binding pocket. Kinase profiling further demonstrated the selectivity of F389-0736 for MAP4K4 across the tested kinase panel. CETSA further demonstrated F389-0736-induced thermal stabilisation of MAP4K4, supporting intracellular target engagement. In pancreatic cancer cells, F389-0736 suppressed TAK1, JNK, and p38 phosphorylation and significantly reduced cell viability and proliferation, with IC50 and GI50 values of 4.41-4.65 μM and 4.03-5.12 μM, respectively. F389-0736 also inhibited clonogenic growth and induced sub-G1 accumulation with activation of apoptotic signalling. RNA sequencing identified 398 differentially expressed genes and revealed enrichment of inflammatory and stress response pathways, programmed cell death programs, oncogenic signalling perturbation, and metabolic reprogramming. These findings identify F389-0736 as a potent and selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor and support its use as a chemical probe and lead scaffold for investigating MAP4K4-dependent signalling and therapeutic vulnerability in pancreatic cancer.

title: Multiomics Profiling Supports Cathepsin B as a Protective Factor in White Matter Hyperintensities and Cognition.
abstract: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are a common brain magnetic resonance imaging marker of cerebral small vessel disease and a major risk factor for stroke and dementia, yet the molecular mechanisms governing lesion formation remain incompletely understood. We sought to identify circulating proteins that lie upstream of WMH and influence related clinical manifestations. We conducted a 4-stage proteogenomic study. Stage 1 tested a WMH polygenic risk score against 2923 plasma proteins in 52 560 UK Biobank participants (mean age, 56.8 years, 53.9% female, 94.0% White), and candidate proteins against WMH volume in the neuroimaging subset (n=5443; mean age 54.2 years, 53.5% female). Stage 2 applied bidirectional Mendelian randomization, colocalization, and local genetic correlation using cis protein quantitative trait locus and cis expression quantitative trait locus instruments from plasma, vascular, and brain tissue. Stage 3 analyzed single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 8 postmortem periventricular white matter samples (4 WMH lesions, 4 controls; mean age, 81 years; 50% female). Stage 4 tested circulating and genetically predicted protein levels against general cognitive ability. Stages 1 and 2 converged on CTSB (cathepsin B) and ECHDC3 (enoyl-coenzyme A hydratase domain-containing 3). Higher plasma CTSB was associated with lower WMH volume (β=-0.09 [95% CI, -0.13 to -0.05]; n=5260), and Mendelian randomization estimates were directionally consistent across all 5 instrument sets (plasma protein quantitative trait locus β=-0.052 [95% CI, -0.064 to -0.040]), with concordant effects on white matter microstructure, perivascular spaces, and lacunar stroke. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing showed CTSB downregulation within lesions, predominantly in astrocytes (log2 fold change=-1.70) and oligodendrocytes (log2 fold change=-0.48; both false discovery rate P<1×10-20). Higher plasma CTSB (β=0.061 [95% CI, 0.010-0.112]; n=5193) and a cis protein quantitative trait locus polygenic score (β=0.031 [95% CI, 0.009-0.054]; n=8884) predicted better cognitive performance. ECHDC3 showed no consistent association beyond stage 1. Multimodal proteogenomic evidence nominates CTSB as a lesion-suppressed protein associated with lower WMH burden and better cognition, and a candidate therapeutic target for cerebral small vessel disease.

title: Sex Differences in Hepatic VLDLR Response to Protein Restriction and Its Relationship with Hepatic Lipid Accumulation.
abstract: Background/Objectives: The very low-density lipoprotein receptor (VLDLR) mediates VLDL uptake in peripheral tissues. This study investigated sex differences in hepatic VLDLR response to protein restriction and its relationship with hepatic lipid accumulation. Methods: Male and female wild-type (WT) and Vldlr knockout (KO) mice were fed control (20% protein) or low-protein (2% protein) diets for 20 days. Hepatic VLDLR expression and triglyceride levels were determined, followed by RNA sequencing and Gene Ontology (GO) analysis. Results: Hepatic Vldlr mRNA and protein levels were higher in females than in males. Protein restriction induced 9-fold and 2.5-fold increases in Vldlr mRNA and VLDLR protein, respectively, in males, whereas females showed only a 1.6-fold increase in VLDLR protein without significant Vldlr mRNA induction. The ATF4 target genes Asns and Fgf21 responded similarly to protein restriction in both sexes. Although females had higher hepatic triglyceride levels than males, this difference persisted in Vldlr KO mice. RNA sequencing revealed sex-dependent effects of Vldlr knockout on hepatic gene expression, with inflammation- and immune-related terms predominantly identified in females. Conclusions: Sex differences in hepatic VLDLR expression do not account for sex differences in hepatic lipid accumulation. The sex-dependent VLDLR response to protein restriction may involve mechanisms other than differential ATF4 activation. Vldlr deficiency was associated with sex-dependent hepatic gene expression changes, particularly those involved in inflammation- and immune-related functions in females. These findings suggest that hepatic VLDLR may have functions beyond its established role in lipoprotein uptake and lipid metabolism and may be relevant to sex-dependent hepatic responses to low-protein nutrition.

title: Targeting of Oral Bacterial Taxa Linked to Disease by Flavonols.
abstract: Networks of different bacterial taxa contribute to oral health. Antibacterials ideally would selectively modulate the subset of bacteria contributing to disease. Plant-derived natural compounds have been shown to inhibit planktonic bacteria or monospecies oral biofilms. However, very few in vivo studies are available to demonstrate the effects of these antimicrobials against native biofilms found in the human oral cavity. The objective of this study was to test putative antibacterials for their ability to affect specific bacterial taxa in complex biofilms. Oral biofilms from donors were collected from saliva then rapidly prepared for polyphenol testing. They were then incubated with test polyphenols for 4 h. 16S rRNA was measured using NGS cDNA sequencing to determine potential targets of bacterial inhibition. Two flavonols, kaempferol and quercetin, had small inhibitory effects on total RNA levels while myricetin at the higher concentration tested, 1 mM, showed substantial inhibition. Effects on the overall microbial population structure as evidenced by alpha diversity of the oral biofilm 16S rRNA were minimal. Remarkably, the flavonols specifically lowered rRNA levels of oral bacterial species associated with both periodontal disease and cardiovascular disease while sparing many commensal bacteria taxa. In sum, plant-derived flavonols are a potential source of selective antimicrobial compounds against oral pathogens and bacteria that may contribute to systemic disease with minimal disruption of overall bacterial activity levels.

title: ISG15 Is a Key Multidirectional Regulator of Cytosolic RNA- and DNA-Sensing Pathways and Type I Interferon Feedback Loops.
abstract: Activation of cytosolic RNA and DNA sensing pathways that normally recognize viral nucleic acids triggers the expression and release of type I interferons (IFN-I). This release drives the expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) that activate acute inflammation and counteract viral replication at various stages. Recent studies have highlighted how interferon-stimulated gene 15 (ISG15), a small, ubiquitin-like modifier, regulates cytosolic RNA and DNA sensing pathway proteins to control the antiviral response and inflammation. ISG15 is a multifunctional protein that acts as a secreted cytokine, binds freely to intracellular proteins, and covalently modifies proteins in a reversible process termed ISGylation. A dual regulatory molecule, ISG15 can both stabilize and destabilize proteins that promote and inhibit IFN-I signaling. Conversely, viruses have evolved strategies to disrupt and exploit ISG15-dependent antiviral responses to evade the host immune system. In this review, we examine how ISG15 regulates cytosolic RNA and DNA sensing pathway proteins to control IFN-I signaling and the antiviral response, highlighting it as a master regulator that fine-tunes IFN-I signaling and feedback. Recognizing the multifaceted action of ISG15 is essential for designing balanced therapeutic strategies across antiviral drug development, cancer immunotherapy, and chronic inflammatory disease management.

title: Computational Investigation of S781F Mutation-Induced Remodeling of the Staphylococcal Nuclease Domain-Containing Protein 1-Argonaute 2 Interface.
abstract: MicroRNA (miRNA)-guided gene silencing depends on the accurate assembly and regulation of the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), in which Argonaute-2 (Ago2) interacts with accessory proteins to facilitate complex stability and catalytic activity. Staphylococcal nuclease domain-containing protein 1 (SND1) is an important component of the RISC and a transcriptional co-regulator implicated in multiple cancers; however, the structural consequences of disease-associated SND1 mutations remain poorly understood. In this study, an integrated computational workflow combining protein-protein docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and free energy analyses was employed to investigate the potential structural effects of the SND1 S781F mutation on the SND1-Ago2 interaction. The wild-type complex was predicted to maintain a stable interaction network involving the Tudor domain of SND1 and methylated arginine residues of Ago2. In contrast, the S781F substitution was associated with altered intermolecular hydrogen bonding patterns, reduced predicted interaction stability, increased structural flexibility, altered correlated residue motions, and a broader free energy landscape, suggesting a less stable protein-protein interface. Although the mutant complex sampled a larger number of distinct intermolecular hydrogen bond interactions, these interactions exhibited lower occupancies and reduced persistence than those in the wild-type complex. Collectively, these computational findings suggest that the S781F mutation could act as a potential modulator of the local physicochemical environment, interaction stability, and conformational dynamics of the SND1-Ago2 surface. This study provides atomistic insights into the structural consequences of the S781F mutation and establishes a computational framework for future experimental validation of its role in miRNA-mediated gene regulation and cancer biology.

title: Advanced Drug Delivery in Pediatric Neurology: Developmental Barriers, Nanocarrier Strategies, and Translational Challenges.
abstract: Treating neurological disorders in children is particularly challenging due to the dynamic maturation of the developing brain, age-dependent pharmacokinetics, and evolving structural and functional properties of the blood-brain barrier (BBB). This review explores the latest advances in drug-delivery systems tailored for pediatric neurology, emphasizing strategies to address physiological and developmental determinants of treatment response across infancy, childhood, and adolescence. The paper begins by outlining the distinct challenges of drug delivery in children, focusing on BBB maturation, transporter expression, metabolic capacity, and neurodevelopmental vulnerability. Emerging delivery systems, such as liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, dendrimers, micelles, gold nanoparticles, and gene- and RNA-based vectors, are further reviewed in relation to major pediatric neurological conditions. These platforms demonstrate promise in enhancing drug bioavailability, targeting specific brain regions, and minimizing systemic toxicity. This paper also covers important safety, regulatory, and ethical considerations in pediatric populations, with a focus on the need for age-appropriate design and thorough clinical validation. Concluding with emerging trends and future directions, this work serves as a comprehensive resource for advancing pediatric neurological therapeutics through state-of-the-art drug delivery technologies.

title: Development and Application of a Dual-Fluorescent Reporter Assay for Feline Infectious Peritonitis Virus RNA-Dependent RNA Polymerase Inhibitor Screening.
abstract: Feline infectious peritonitis virus (FIPV) causes a fatal disease in cats that remains challenging to treat due to the absence of effective vaccines and limited antiviral therapies. Given its central role in viral replication and transcription, RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) represents a highly promising and strategic target for antiviral drug development. To enable live-cell monitoring of RdRp activity without external substrates or cell disruption, we developed a biologically validated, cell-based dual-fluorescent reporter assay using green fluorescent protein and red fluorescent protein to evaluate RdRp-dependent reporter activity. Following validation with the well-characterized RdRp inhibitor ribavirin, the dual-reporter platform achieved a Z-factor of 0.54 and a Z'-factor of 0.61. The system was further utilized to assess the antiviral potential of fifteen alkaloid compounds. Among compounds evaluated, lycorine and lycorine hydrochloride exhibited potent inhibition of RdRp-dependent reporter activity and yielded IC50 values of 2.83 ± 0.45 μM and 1.58 ± 0.20 μM, respectively. Further evaluation revealed that both compounds significantly reduced FIPV replication in infected cell. These findings identify lycorine and lycorine hydrochloride as promising anti-FIPV candidates and support further investigation of lycorine-class alkaloids as anti-coronaviral scaffolds. Together, the validated cell-based screening platform and whole-virus antiviral activity provide a foundation for advancing RdRp-targeted antiviral discovery against FIPV.

title: In Silico Pre-Screening as a Design-Assessment Tool for Gold Nanoparticle-Amplified DNA Displacement Assays: Identifying Sequence-Level Design Limitations Across Electrode and Magnetic-Bead Configurations.
abstract: The growing demand for decentralised and point-of-care (POC) nucleic acid testing has increased interest in label-free, sequence-specific DNA biosensors and computational approaches that can guide their design before extensive experimental optimisation. Here, an in silico workflow was first employed to evaluate a gold nanoparticle (AuNP)-amplified, target-induced DNA displacement assay. Nearest-neighbour duplex thermodynamics, DNA secondary-structure analysis, and High Ambiguity Driven biomolecular DOCKing (HADDOCK) were used to assess sequence complementarity and displacement behaviour. The analyses confirmed Watson-Crick complementarity among the electrode capture, reporter, and target sequences and identified an unintended mismatch in the magnetic bead-capture probe. HADDOCK analyses using default RNA and explicit DNA settings consistently favoured target over non-target displacement, although control poses were more setting-sensitive. Experimental testing subsequently provided supporting evidence for the computational assessment. Electrochemical measurements showed the anticipated signal hierarchy of target > non-target > buffer, although differences were not statistically significant at the replicate numbers tested. The magnetic bead platform produced weak, non-differential responses, consistent with the sequence-level design limitation identified computationally. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of computational pre-screening for interrogating displacement mechanisms, identifying correctable design errors, and guiding rational experimental optimisation of nucleic acid biosensors. No statistically significant target discrimination was achieved at the replicate numbers tested, and the proposed corrected bead-capture sequence has not been experimentally validated.

title: Flipons, Noncoding Transcripts and Retroelements: A Universal Host Defense.
abstract: Encoding genetic information involves both structure and sequence. Non-protein-coding (NCR) RNAs modulate host immune responses by guiding and assembling stress-specific protein effectors, with flipons enabling dynamic transitions between states. Small NCRs transcribed by both RNA Polymerases 2 and 3 normally modulate these pathways. The miRNAs, tRNA fragments, mitrons, piRNAs, and endo-small-interfering RNA products target the guide effector complexes to their targets. These NCRs filter the subset of RNAs that are translated, a process modulated by other NCRs that fine-tune RNA stability, localization, and kinetics through the modifications they direct. When these RNAs, or their targets, are dysregulated, host interferon responses are activated through the accumulation of uncapped triphosphorylated RNAs, dsRNAs, or flipon-encoded Z-RNAs. These responses are initially suppressed to avoid attacks on self-RNAs, but above a threshold, highly immunogenic pathways are unleashed. These same responses resist viral and other infections without pathogen-specific effectors or prior exposure. They also eliminate dysfunctional cells. These universal responses, when unresolved, contribute to a range of pathologies, increasing cancer, inflammatory diseases, and senescence. The review focuses on recent findings showing how these integrated host responses are driven by, and exploit, the retrotransposon invasion of animal genomes.

title: The Structure, Evolution, and Comparative Genomics of the Dendrobium officinale Mitochondrial Genome.
abstract: Dendrobium officinale is an important medicinal Orchidaceae species with considerable ecological and economic value. While its chloroplast genome has been well characterized, the structure features of its mitochondrial genome remain largely unexplored, which further hinders our understanding of its evolutionary dynamics and adaptive mechanisms. This study presents a comprehensive characterization of the mitochondrial genome of D. officinale, revealing a complex multibranched structure of 22 chromosomes totaling 639,931 bp, encoding 35 PCGs, 3 rRNA genes, and 24 tRNA genes. Codon usage analysis revealed a distinct codon bias, while the genome harbors abundant repetitive elements and 522 RNA editing sites. Comparative genomic analysis identified 125 MTPT fragments totaling 108,012 bp (16.88% of the mitogenome), indicating frequent inter-organellar DNA transfer. Dendrobium nobile exhibited the highest genomic homology with D. officinale. Ka/Ks analysis indicated that most mitochondrial genes are under strong purifying selection. In addition, we conducted a comparative analysis between the newly assembled mitochondrial genome of D. officinale and seven Orchidaceae species. Phylogenetic analysis based on the maximum likelihood, maximum parsimony and bayesian inference approaches resolved the phylogenetic position of D. officinale within Orchidaceae. Collectively, these findings provide a valuable reference for future studies on Orchidaceae phylogenomics and mitochondrial evolution.

title: Recovering Small Molecule Ligand-RNA Binding Pocket Binding Modes and Exploring Potential Binding Pathways Using Metadynamics.
abstract: Understanding how an RNA recognizes small molecule ligands is crucial for pharmaceutical research. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can potentially reveal this process in atomistic detail. However, simulations frequently fail should energy barriers along the pathway prove to be insurmountably high on the simulation timescale (ns-µs). To address this limitation, we present a novel strategy combining well-tempered metadynamics utilizing X-ray crystallography or NMR-solved hydrogen-bonding interactions between an RNA and its ligand as collective variables (CVs). This approach can sample multiple transitions during the binding process and determine the most favorable binding modes through the reconstructed free energy landscape. Our computational recovery of binding modes for all five cases studied is in good agreement (RMSD below 2.0 Å) with the experimentally determined structures of the bound complexes. Our study demonstrates that metadynamics coupled with strategically chosen collective variables can effectively sample binding pathways and recover binding modes for RNA-small molecule complexes. This method therefore could be valuable for crystal structure interpretation, NMR solution structure refinement, and computer-aided design of RNA-targeted small molecule drugs.

title: DNA and mRNA Vaccines Against Hantaviruses: Antigen Design, Delivery Strategies and Translational Progress.
abstract: Hantaviruses are members of the Hantaviridae family, which can cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). At present, no specific antiviral treatment is available for hantavirus infection, while licensed hantavirus vaccines are restricted to a limited number of countries in Asia. This review summarizes recent advances in hantavirus deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines, focusing on antigen design, delivery systems, immunogenicity, safety and translational development. Peer-reviewed studies published primarily within the past 10 years were evaluated together with available hantavirus vaccine trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov, with emphasis on Hantaan virus (HTNV), Puumala virus (PUUV) and Andes virus (ANDV). DNA vaccine candidates have demonstrated immunogenicity in preclinical and early clinical studies, with an acceptable safety profile. mRNA vaccines represent a newer approach with promising preclinical evidence of humoral and cellular immune responses. However, they have not yet been evaluated clinically. Studies have also reported the potential for varying degrees of cross-protection between hantavirus species, although protection remains limited by antigenic diversity. Overall, current evidence supports further development of nucleic acid-based hantavirus vaccines, particularly multivalent strategies, with emphasis on standardized evaluation and clinical efficacy.

title: It takes two to tango: the intersection of deubiquitinases and m6A modification in cancer.
abstract: The dynamic and reversible N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modification has emerged as a pivotal layer of epitranscriptomic regulation in cancer, governing RNA metabolism and function. Concurrently, deubiquitylating enzymes (DUBs), key components of the post-translational modifications (PTMs) system, orchestrate protein stability and signaling pathways crucial for tumorigenesis. Recent evidence reveals extensive and intricate crosstalk between these two regulatory systems, forming a complex network that can influence cancer progression. This review systematically explores the bidirectional interplay between DUBs and m6A modification. On one hand, specific DUBs can deubiquitinate and stabilize core m6A "writers" (methyltransferases), "erasers" (demethylases), or "readers" (recognition proteins), thereby influencing RNA metabolism and downstream gene expression. On the other hand, m6A modification can regulate the expression of certain DUBs, either by influencing the stability and translation of their mRNAs or by controlling associated regulatory factors. This reciprocal regulation profoundly impacts key oncogenic processes, including cell proliferation, metastasis, metabolic reprogramming, and therapy resistance. By integrating current findings, this review highlights the significance of the DUB-m6A axis as a critical regulatory hub in cancer biology. Deciphering this crosstalk not only provides novel insights into tumor mechanisms but also unveils promising therapeutic targets for overcoming drug resistance and developing innovative anti-cancer strategies.

title: Human brain evolution: Role of SINE-VNTR-Alu retrotransposons and SINE-VNTR-Alu long noncoding RNA AK057321.
abstract: Humans differ remarkably from great apes, with advanced cognitive abilities correlated to enlarged brains resulting from prolonged neurodevelopment. The SINE-VNTR-Alu (SVA) retrotransposons are candidate genetic drivers of these differences. Human genes with intronic SVAs are enriched for neurodevelopmental diseases; the microcephaly gene CDK5 regulatory subunit associated protein 2 (CDK5RAP2) and epilepsy/intellectual disability gene SCN8A coding for sodium channel subunit contain human-specific, intronic SVAs. Deleting gene ZNF91 coding for the SVA-binding zinc finger protein 91 or the intronic SVAs upregulate gene expression to accelerate functional and structural neuron maturation. We also discovered the function of AK057321, duplicated in ultrarare autism, founding a new gene family of long noncoding RNAs containing SVA sequences. AK057321 increases 10-fold as progenitors mature into glutamatergic neurons, and its premature increase upregulates CDK5RAP2 and SCN8A to accelerate neuron maturation. As anticipated by its sequence complementarity, AK057321 forms RNA:DNA heteroduplexes with genomic SVAs and decoy-binds the ZNF91 repressive complex. SVA-mediated block of CDK5RAP2-induced neuron maturation could prolong progenitor proliferation to increase neuron numbers and cerebral cortex size. SVA-lncRNA AK057321 also acts in adulthood to promote threefold enriched expression of Huntington (containing an SVA) in the frontal cortex relative to the brain stem. The large number of neurologic genes regulated by SVA-lncRNA AK057321 suggests the retrotransposon-based gene regulatory mechanism shaped human brain development and functions to advance cognitive abilities.

title: The impact of genetic mutations in epigenetic factors on brain development and neurodevelopmental disorders.
abstract: Brain development is tightly controlled at many different levels that work in harmony to ensure the proper structure and function of brain cells. Such regulatory processes act at the level of genomic DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) composition and fundamental cellular events that control gene transcription, transcript processing/alternative splicing, and protein translation. Both genetics and epigenetics control the gene expression program of every single cell, the latter referring to the regulatory processes that are not reflected in the order of DNA sequences. Epigenetic regulation mainly includes modification of DNA molecules (DNA methylation) or chemical changes in amino acid residues of DNA-bound proteins (histone posttranslational modifications). The combination of DNA and histone proteins constitutes the chromatin. The crosstalk between DNA and histone proteins and their different epigenetic modifications affects chromatin organization, resulting in active and inactive chromatin compartments. Importantly, genetic mutation of epigenetic factors may impact the process of brain development and function throughout life. In this chapter, we will focus on epigenetic factors that are involved in DNA methylation and histone modifications, known as "writers, readers, and erasers/modifiers." A brief section is also included on regulatory RNA (ribonucleic acid) molecules that may impact gene expression. Lastly, we will provide some context on the impact of genetic mutations on epigenetic factors that may lead to neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Decoding the ncRNA Script: Elucidation of Major Host Regulatory lncRNAs and circRNAs Shaping RNA Virus Pathogenesis.
abstract: Viruses are key infectious agents causing large-scale mortality among humans every year with the recent example of the devastating COVID-19 pandemic. RNA viruses are often associated with higher pathogenicity and their molecular mechanisms of entry into host cells, replication, transmission, and propagation remain poorly understood. To facilitate virus replication and propagation, these viruses regulate the host gene transcription and translation, key cellular processes like apoptosis, autophagy, innate as well as adaptive immune responses, lipid biosynthesis, and other key host signaling processes. They hijack and exploit the host cell machinery by modulating the expression of host proteins and ncRNAs. Some of the regulatory RNAs that these viruses modulate involve lncRNAs, circRNAs and ceRNA networks. RNA viruses alter or control key cellular processes of these RNAs by directly or indirectly interacting with both host and viral proteins and other non-coding RNAs. Through the alteration of regulation of non-coding RNAs, the viruses have been demonstrated to alter several biological processes primarily metabolic pathways, inflammation, and immune pathways like interferon signaling and other innate immune pathways to aid virus replication, pathogenesis and immune evasion. These differentially expressed regulatory RNAs can be further studied to develop potential antiviral therapeutics and vaccines. CeRNA networks involve the role of protein-coding mRNAs and competing ncRNAs like lncRNA, miRNA, and circRNA. This review explores some of the reported modulations of host lncRNAs, circRNAs, and ceRNA networks in RNA virus infections to understand their importance and role in virus pathogenesis.

title: Bisphenol A induces hepatotoxicity via a LAMP3-dependent impairment of mitophagic processing and reduced PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling.
abstract: Bisphenol A (BPA) is a ubiquitous environmental toxicant, but the mechanisms underlying BPA-associated hepatic injury remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the involvement of lysosome-associated membrane protein 3 (LAMP3) in mitophagy-related alterations and downstream survival signaling. Human hepatocellular carcinoma-derived Huh7 and PLC5 cells and a mouse model of 4-week BPA exposure were used. Cell proliferation and apoptosis were assessed using CCK-8, EdU, TUNEL, and flow cytometry; mitochondrial function and morphology were evaluated using JC-1, MitoTracker, reactive oxygen species detection, and transmission electron microscopy. RNA sequencing identified BPA-responsive genes, followed by LAMP3 loss- and gain-of-function experiments and chloroquine (CQ) treatment. BPA exposure was associated with proliferative arrest, apoptosis, mitochondrial dysfunction, increased oxidative stress, accumulation of acidic vesicular organelles, an increased LC3B-II/I ratio, and p62 accumulation-a pattern consistent with impaired late-stage mitophagic processing. LAMP3 was strongly upregulated after BPA exposure. LAMP3 silencing attenuated mitochondrial and cellular injury, reduced p62, increased LysoTracker signal, and increased PI3K-AKT-mTOR phosphorylation; CQ attenuated these protective changes. Conversely, LAMP3 overexpression aggravated BPA-associated injury and produced marker changes consistent with impaired autophagic processing. Together, these findings support LAMP3 as a contributor to BPA-associated cellular injury in the Huh7 and PLC5 models studied and suggest an association between LAMP3-related lysosomal alterations, impaired mitophagic processing, and reduced PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling. Because dynamic mitophagic flux was not directly measured and LAMP3 was not targeted in vivo, the proposed pathway requires confirmation using tandem flux reporters, primary human hepatocytes, and in vivo genetic models.

title: Functional diversification of the cephalopod proteome by RNA editing.
abstract: Coleoid cephalopods exhibit the highest levels of adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR)-mediated RNA editing of any known taxon, yet the functional consequences of most recoding events remain unclear. Here, we integrated proteomics with biochemical and cellular assays to characterize recoding across the Doryteuthis pealeii proteome. This confirmed the translation of 7,997 recoded sites at the protein level and revealed how recoding reshapes the proteome by altering protein stability, subcellular localization, post-translational modifications, and enzymatic activity. We find that recoding also creates or ablates post-translational modification sites, with direct effects on protein function and protein-protein interactions. Recoding the E3 ligase MARCHF5 drives widespread changes in substrate ubiquitylation and perturbs mitochondrial homeostasis, illustrating how RNA editing can influence organelle function. Together, these data give a proteome-scale view of how extensive RNA recoding diversifies protein function in coleoid cephalopods and offer a framework for understanding how RNA-level plasticity shapes protein function and cellular physiology.

title: c-di-GMP targets the enhancer-binding protein SfnR1 to regulate Pseudomonas aeruginosa growth under sulfur limitation.
abstract: As a ubiquitous bacterial second messenger, cyclic di-GMP (c-di-GMP) governs diverse physiological processes by directly binding to transcriptional regulators or other effector proteins. Enhancer-binding proteins (EBPs) are a distinct class of transcriptional regulators that, together with σ54-RNA polymerase, promote downstream gene expression through ATP hydrolysis. To date, no EBP other than FleQ has been reported to interact with c-di-GMP in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. By systematically screening P. aeruginosa EBPs for c-di-GMP binding, we identified SfnR1 as a novel receptor. SfnR1 is known to promote msuEDC and sfnG expression, enabling bacteria to utilize nonpreferred sulfur sources (including DMSO and DMSO2) under sulfur limitation. However, whether SfnR1 is regulated by c-di-GMP and how this regulation affects its transcriptional activity remain unknown. Here, we demonstrate that c-di-GMP binding to SfnR1 prevents SfnR1 from binding to the msuEDC and sfnG promoters, thereby downregulating their expression. This impairs P. aeruginosa assimilation of nonpreferred sulfur sources and ultimately restricts its growth under sulfur-limiting conditions. In contrast, modulation of c-di-GMP levels in P. aeruginosa has no effect on growth under normal conditions. Collectively, our findings establish that c-di-GMP binding to SfnR1 selectively restricts P. aeruginosa growth under sulfur limitation, uncovering a novel mechanism whereby this second messenger modulates bacterial adaptation to nutrient stress.

title: Mechanisms underlying biomaterial-regulated macrophage polarization in bone tissue engineering: From interface sensing to immune microenvironment remodeling.
abstract: Traditional biomaterials commonly trigger a foreign body reaction after implantation, leading to fibrous encapsulation and poor osseointegration. Advances in osteoimmunology have enabled contemporary tissue engineering to redefine biomaterials as active modulators of the osteoimmune microenvironment rather than as passive scaffolds. At the core of this reconceptualization is the targeted control of macrophage polarization to establish an immune environment conducive to bone repair. The plasticity of macrophages reflects the dynamic balance between the M1 pro-inflammatory and M2 pro-regenerative states; this plasticity ultimately determines regenerative outcomes. This review offers a conceptual four-dimensional regulatory framework that extends from extracellular interface sensing to intracellular genome remodeling and progresses from material properties and signaling cascade stratification to mitochondrial reprogramming and non-coding RNA (ncRNA) networks. Within this framework, material interfaces function as platforms for activating, transducing, and integrating bioactive signals. These signals can be externally modulated to reshape intracellular metabolic organization and sustain mitochondrial function. At a finer regulatory tier, ncRNAs modulate signaling pathways to achieve the precise post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression. Central to this model is a bidirectional, spatiotemporally dynamic feedback loop linking intrinsic cellular machinery with extrinsic material systems. Linking material design parameters to dynamic biological responses lays a conceptual foundation for the development of biomaterials capable of the adaptive and programmable regulation of the osteoimmune microenvironment. Future research may focus on the precise temporal control of M1/M2 phenotypic switching and the coordinated presentation of multiple signals, thereby advancing the development of next-generation immunomodulatory biomaterials for bone repair.

title: Discovery of novel CDK9 inhibitors containing 1H-pyrrolo[2,3-b]pyridine moiety for treatment of colorectal cancer.
abstract: In this work, YK-2168 was selected as the lead compound for the development of a series of highly selective CDK9 inhibitors due to its unique 1H-pyrrolo[2,3-b]pyridine scaffold, which acts as an optimal backbone for targeting the kinase hinge region. The optimized compound B3 exhibited potent inhibitory activities at both enzymatic and cellular levels with satisfactory selectivity. Mechanistic studies revealed that compound B3 induces apoptosis in the HCT116 cells by suppressing the phosphorylation of RNA polymerase II at Ser2 site, which further results in the downregulates the expression of apoptosis-related gene and protein (Mcl-1) and triggers the cleavage of caspase 3 and PARP. Pharmacokinetic studies and in vivo experiments demonstrated that intravenous injection of compound B3 could achieve prominent therapeutic efficacy with a high safety profile. In general, these findings indicate that compound B3 is a promising candidate for CRC treatment.

title: Regulation of target gene expression by chromatin-associated protein-coding transcripts in plants.
abstract: Protein-coding transcripts are regarded as intermediates that mediate DNA-to-protein information flow, leaving their noncoding regulatory potential largely underappreciated. Genome-wide profiling of RNA-chromatin interactions in Arabidopsis has uncovered widespread associations between protein-coding transcripts and distinct genomic loci, implying that they possess regulatory functions. Here, we found that BT2 and GSL8 transcripts modulate target gene transcription independently of their protein products through distinct mechanisms. The BT2 transcript represses transcription of its targets CEP2 and MRF4 by forming RNA-DNA triplexes, thereby restricting root growth and promoting flowering, whereas GSL8 acts through a triplex-independent pathway. Our findings unveil intrinsic regulatory activities of protein-coding transcripts, challenging the canonical definition of mRNA function and blurring the functional distinction between coding and noncoding RNAs in the context of genome evolution.

title: A broad-host-range Rhizobium rhizogenes strain enables transient expression across diverse crop species.
abstract: Agrobacterium-mediated transient expression has revolutionised plant research, enabling numerous landmark discoveries across diverse areas of plant biology. Yet this powerful approach remains largely confined to solanaceous species, leaving most economically important crop families without a comparable rapid assay platform. Here, we show that an engineered Rhizobium rhizogenes strain, AS109, mediates efficient transient expression across diverse dicot species spanning multiple taxonomic families, consistently outperforming commonly used laboratory agrobacterial strains. Leveraging the broad host range of AS109, we establish a suite of functional assays in faba bean (Vicia faba), including protein localisation, RNA interference-mediated gene silencing, cell-surface elicitor recognition screens, nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptor (NLR) activation, and infection cell biology at the host-pathogen interface. We further demonstrate that both singleton NLRs and sensor-helper NLR pairs from Solanaceae retain effector recognition and cell death activity when transferred into faba bean, establishing a rapid platform for evaluating cross-family transferability of disease-resistance genes. AS109 thus provides an accessible and versatile chassis for functional genomics in non-model crops, bridging the widening gap between hypothesis generation and experimental validation across diverse plant species.

title: The NuRD complex shapes RNA polymerase III activity at highly expressed tRNA gene clusters, tuning the dynamic range of cellular tRNA pools.
abstract: RNA polymerase III (Pol III) transcription produces RNAs involved in core biological processes and is therefore coupled to fluctuating demands for protein synthesis and cell growth. However, the mechanisms underlying dynamic Pol III regulation remain incompletely understood. To address this gap, we investigated protein-protein interactions shared across multiple Pol III subunits to characterize the macromolecular interactome of Pol III, with special attention directed toward potential regulatory factors. Our survey uncovers interactions between Pol III and the NuRD (nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase) complex. We further show that NuRD localizes to active Pol III-transcribed genes, including tRNA gene clusters associated with notably high expression. Inhibiting NuRD-associated deacetylase activity increases Pol III transcription at these sites, suggesting that NuRD constrains Pol III activity and thereby modulates the dynamic range of Pol III-derived RNAs. These findings implicate NuRD as a chromatin-based mechanism linking signaling events and metabolic need with the dynamic availability of specific tRNA pools.

title: Long Noncoding RNA: An Uncharted Territory in Plant Diseases and Immunity.
abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) are a class of transcripts longer than 200 nucleotides with little or no protein-coding capacity. They represent a substantial fraction of eukaryotic genomes and function as molecular architects that coordinate diverse biological processes and physiological plasticity, including multilayered plant defence systems, through versatile regulatory interactions at multiple levels of gene regulation. Recent advances in high-throughput RNA sequencing technologies have greatly expanded the identification of plant lncRNAs, revealing their diverse roles as scaffolds, decoys, guides, and regulatory molecules. These lncRNAs are increasingly recognised as integral components of plant immune systems, contributing critically to host defence mechanisms. This review highlights recent progress in lncRNA identification using computational pipelines as well as emerging artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) based approaches. We further explore current insights into the regulatory functions of lncRNAs during host-pathogen interactions. Notably, we discuss a paradigm-shifting discovery in lncRNA biology, the finding that many lncRNAs, once presumed to be non-coding, contain small open reading frames (sORFs) that encode functional micropeptides. Modern predictive modelling has been crucial to identify these sORFs and their peptide products and to show that lncRNAs have multiple functions as regulatory transcripts and peptide precursors in plant immunity.

title: Metabolic links between mitochondrial electron transport, glycolysis, and AMP-activated protein kinase signaling modulate hepatocellular carcinoma cell survival.
abstract: Beyond ATP production, mitochondrial metabolism, due to its essential role in cell proliferation and survival, is a potential target for cancer therapy. However, translation into clinical practice is challenging owing to several limitations, including difficulty in distinguishing cancerous and non-cancerous mitochondria, which is further complicated by the heterogeneity of the former. Herein, we focused on cancerous mitochondria exhibiting low DNA/RNA levels and respiratory function compared with those demonstrated by normal cells, and determined the effects of low respiratory activity on the metabolic phenotypes of cancer cells. Interestingly, mitochondria low-type (mt-Low) cells derived from hepatocellular carcinomas were relatively sensitive to electron transport chain (ETC) inhibition. Specifically, cells died under the treatment with the ETC inhibitors, rotenone and antimycin A, at lower doses compared with cells exhibiting normal respiratory activity (mt-psNormal), although ATP levels were sustained in both cell types under these conditions. In mt-psNormal cells, upon ETC inhibition, glycolytic activity increased, and AMP-activated protein kinase was activated, which critically contributed to cell survival. However, these responses were not effectively induced in ETC inhibition-sensitive mt-Low cells. Similar to conventional ETC inhibitors, small interfering RNAs targeting core subunits of respiratory complexes I or III effectively inhibited proliferation (complexes I and III) or survival (complex I) of the tested mt-Low cancer cells, supporting innovative anticancer approaches that target respiratory function using next-generation technology.

title: A research on machine learning based gene selection algorithms for RNA-seq data.
abstract: Discovering differentially expressed genes (DEGs) is an essential process for diagnosis and treatment. In this study, we evaluate the capacity of machine learning algorithms to identify genes that are simulated as truly differentially expressed. We first obtain nine real datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas Program. We conduct Monte Carlo simulation by exploring the characteristics of the real datasets (i.e. the number of genes). Since these datasets have highly imbalanced class distributions, datasets with the same characteristics are also generated with balanced class ratios. In this way, 18 scenarios are obtained with a total number of 19,947 genes of which 10 genes are simulated significantly different between the two groups. After the pre-processing steps including filtering, normalization, transformation and univariate analysis, gene selection is conducted with five machine learning algorithms. These are biosigner algorithm, GMDH-type neural network algorithm, Determan's optimal gene selection algorithm with random forest, support vector machines and elastic net generalized linear models. Five-fold cross validation is used for improving gene selection performances. Recall, precision and F-measure are taken into account for the evaluation of gene selection performances. All algorithms show higher average performance in balanced scenarios than in unbalanced scenarios. Elastic net generally achieves favorable average performance in both balanced and unbalanced scenarios.

title: Co-opted CHIP E3 Ub-ligase provides protein quality control by regulating molecular properties of condensates formed by a positive-strand RNA virus.
abstract: Positive-strand RNA viruses are important pathogens that built viral replication organelles (VROs) via exploiting co-opted host proteins and intracellular membranes in infected cells. Tomato bushy stunt virus (TBSV) membranous VROs are associated with dynamic virus-induced replication (vir)-condensate substructures driven by TBSV p33 replication protein. We targeted micropeptide "killswitch" to VROs to enhance p33 self-association and remodel vir-condensates. Recruitment of killswitch induced p33 aggregations, reduced mobility of co-opted glycolytic enzymes in vir-condensate, limited ATP production within VROs, and inhibited TBSV replication. We discovered that TBSV co-opts CHIP/STUB1 E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in protein quality control to limit detrimental effect of protein aggregations in VROs. Expression of CHIP reduced accumulation of aggregated TBSV p33. Knockdown of CHIP resulted in inhibition of TBSV replication, enhanced accumulation of aggregation-prone p33 mutants, and inhibited mobility of co-opted client host proteins in vir-condensate. Subverted CHIP plays critical role in regulating protein interactions, stability, and maintenance of dynamic vir-condensate. Hijacking protein quality control mechanism is a previously unknown phenomenon during (+)RNA virus replication.

title: MTR4: A Conserved Youth Factor for Vascular Endothelium.
abstract: Vascular endothelial cell (VEC) senescence drives organismal aging and age-related pathologies, yet the intrinsic factors preserving endothelial youthfulness remain poorly defined. Here, we identify MTR4, an evolutionarily conserved RNA helicase and nuclear RNA exosome cofactor, as a novel regulator of VEC senescence. MTR4 protein declines markedly in senescent HUVECs and aged mouse aortas, independent of general cell cycle exit. Mechanistically, senescence-induced upregulation of the E3 ubiquitin ligase synoviolin 1 (SYVN1) promotes K638-linked ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of MTR4. MTR4 depletion drives proliferating HUVECs into premature senescence, whereas its overexpression restores a youthful phenotype in senescent cells by binding BUB3 to stabilize BUB3 and sustain BUBR1 expression. In mice, endothelial Mtr4 knockdown promotes vascular dysfunction and multi-organ aging, while endothelium-specific Mtr4 overexpression alleviates these phenotypes. In C. elegans, mtr-4 overexpression dramatically extends lifespan, comparable to classic longevity models and surpassing most single-gene interventions, while its knockdown accelerates aging. Our findings establish MTR4 as a critical guardian of endothelial homeostasis and organismal aging, with strong translational potential for mitigating age-related vascular dysfunction.

title: FGFR3 Gene Alterations and Protein Expression in Paired TURBT and Radical Cystectomy Archival Specimens of Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer.
abstract: This study investigated whether neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) influences the detectability of fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 gene alterations (FGFR3alt) in muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). Among 173 patients who underwent radical cystectomy (RC), 70 had paired transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) and RC archival specimens available for FGFR3 RNA testing and immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis. FGFR3alt were detected in only six tumors (8.6%), and 13 RC specimens (19%) showed RNA test failure, predominantly in archival samples older than 10 years. The assay-success concordance of FGFR3 RNA test results between paired TURBT and RC specimens was high (73%), although one NAC-treated patient with FGFR3alt TURBT tissue converted to FGFR3-negative status in the RC specimen. IHC analysis demonstrated significantly higher FGFR3 protein expression in FGFR3alt tumors and a moderate correlation between paired TURBT and RC specimens, irrespective of NAC exposure. Because FGFR3 alterations were detected in only a small number of cases, the study was underpowered to evaluate whether NAC influences FGFR3alt detectability. These findings underscore the need for validation in larger, multi-institutional datasets and integrated molecular profiling to clarify the impact of chemotherapy on FGFR3-driven bladder cancer biology.

title: Molecular Characterization and Functional Analysis of Pomacea canaliculata Mos Gene (PcMos): A Molecular Switch of Female Fecundity.
abstract: The invasive Pomacea canaliculata has emerged as a notorious pest that endangers aquatic crops, ecological services and functioning. Although well-documented as a mammalian oocyte maturation factor, the biological roles of Moloney sarcoma oncogene (Mos) in invertebrates, notably P. canaliculata, remain unfathomed. We integrated RNA interference (RNAi)-mediated gene silencing alongside bioinformatic, molecular, biochemical and histological approaches to dissect fecundity-related functions and modulatory mechanisms of PcMos at the mRNA, protein and in silico levels. Characterized by the conserved protein kinase domain and motif, the PcMos protein sequence presented close phylogeny with its molluscan counterparts. Spatiotemporal expression profiling showed that mRNA and protein levels of PcMos were enriched in female adults and ovarian tissues. Efficient in vivo RNAi effects were induced as the transcription and translation of PcMos significantly declined by 78.2% and 79.0%, respectively, following a microinjection of 5 μg dsPcMos per female post 48 h. The downstream MAPK pathway, comprising MEK1, ERK1 and p90RSK1, was depressed when subjected to dsPcMos treatment, as reflected by pronounced decreases in mRNA and phosphorylated protein levels. Substantial diminution of E2/Pg/LH/FSH contents were noticed in the PcMos-RNAi group versus the dsEGFP group, suggesting fundamental implications of PcMos in endocrine regulation. In addition, the concurrent expression and high affinity between PcMos and VTG were visualized by the immunofluorescence and molecular docking, which may be associated with the diminished VTG content and expression upon PcMos silencing. Moreover, PcMos knockdown led to impaired ovarian development and reduced SP content, the number ofmature oocytes, egg production and egg-hatching rates. Taken together, our findings pointed to PcMos as a molecular switch pivotal for female fecundity, potentially acting through coordinated effects on MAPK signaling, endocrine hormone homeostasis and yolk deposition. This study may inspire the precision pest management and inform the design of RNAi-based sterility agents to suppress P. canaliculata populations.

title: Deeply conserved and expressed small ORFs in the model beetle Tribolium castaneum.
abstract: Small open reading frames (small ORFs/smORFs/sORFs) were historically overlooked due to their short length (< 100 codons) and detection challenges. It is widely accepted that small ORFs are rarely conserved across distant taxa, particularly in deeply rooted ancestors. However, growing evidence supports their biological relevance and potential roles in gene innovation. Integrating genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic datasets, we identified and characterized 454 putative small ORFs in Tribolium castaneum. Conservation analyses revealed 230 potential orthologs within Coleoptera, 167 in insects, 85 in arthropods, 39 in eukaryotes, and six in bacteria. Conserved small ORFs displayed higher GC content (~ 44.87%), with bacterial-conserved sequences exceeding 50%. Functional enrichment revealed dozens of small ORFs associated with catalytic, transporter, structural, and regulatory roles. Binding site predictions indicated 254 small ORFs possess protein-protein interaction potential. Expression profiles across 14 RNA-seq libraries spanning multiple developmental stages showed 40.1% of small ORFs expressed (TPM > 1) in at least one sample, and 16.5% expressed in five or more libraries. Conserved small ORFs showed broader, stable expression, while lineage-specific genes displayed restricted expression, mostly in gonads or embryos. Isoformic and small CDSs (coding DNA sequences) were the most widely expressed classes. Notably, 29 small ORFs exhibited transcriptional and translational support (Swiss-Prot/Ribo-seq), 28 being small CDSs. Furthermore, 390 small ORFs had potential paralogs, some homologous to described proteins. Our findings highlight the small ORF diversity and provide a framework for distinguishing conserved small proteins from lineage-specific candidates, emphasizing the need for experimental validation to determine their functional relevance and evolutionary significance.

title: Dynamic myogenic progression of broiler satellite cells during growth and the regulatory role of bone morphogenetic protein 6.
abstract: Satellite cells (SCs) contribute to skeletal muscle hypertrophy and meat yields in broilers. An efficient myogenic process of SCs requires timely-regulated transitions of their cellular states from quiescence to activation and then to differentiation. However, our understanding of these dynamic cellular state transitions during broiler growth and underlying regulatory mechanisms remain limited. We conducted a comprehensive characterization of SCs in Ross 308 broilers from 1 to 42 days post-hatch, using an integrated approach combining in vivo and in vitro analyses with single-nucleus RNA sequencing. The results showed that the ratio of MYOD1+ differentiating SCs decreased with age along with the reduced expression of myogenic regulatory genes, suggesting a decline in myogenic capacity. Consistently, snRNA-seq analysis revealed that the proportion of quiescent SCs increased, while the fractions of proliferating and differentiating SCs decreased during growth. Furthermore, bone morphogenetic protein 6 (BMP6), secreted specifically by the quiescent SCs, acts as a key regulator that maintains SC quiescence and inhibits their activation, accounting for the reduced myogenic differentiation capacity of SCs in the breast muscle of broilers at day 42. In vitro cell culture studies validated that knockdown of BMP6 expression in isolated primary SCs promoted proliferation, differentiation, and myotube formation, while overexpression of BMP6 achieved the opposite effects. Therefore, BMP6 was identified as a key regulatory target for maintaining SC quiescence and inhibiting their activation. These findings further advance our understanding into SCs state transitions during growth and provide a foundation for developing strategies to enhance muscle growth in broilers.

title: NOP58 knockdown in microglia is associated with reduced neuroinflammation and synaptic damage in NMOSD.
abstract: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) is a severe inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. This study investigated the role of nucleolar protein 58 (NOP58) in NMOSD pathogenesis, focusing on microglia-mediated neuroinflammation and synaptic damage. Differentially expressed genes were obtained from the GSE235276 dataset to identify hub genes via support vector machine-recursive feature elimination and protein-protein interaction networks. Diagnostic performance was validated using receiver operating characteristic analysis based on the GSE235277 dataset. BV2 cells treated with serum from NMOSD patients were co-cultured with primary cortical neurons. Molecular effects of NOP58 silencing were assessed using real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction, western blotting, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for inflammatory cytokines, microglial activation markers, and synaptic markers. RNA binding motif protein 28 (RBM28) and NOP58 were identified as candidate hub genes with potential diagnostic value. Both were upregulated in BV2 cells treated with NMOSD serum and confirmed in serum-derived RNA from NMOSD patients. The treatment of the serum from patients with NMOSD significantly increased pro-inflammatory cytokines (interleukin [IL]-1β, IL-6, tumor necrosis factor-α) and the expression of Iba1 in BV2 cells. NOP58 expression positively correlated with these cytokines. NOP58 silencing reduced cytokine levels, restored postsynaptic density protein 95 (PSD95) and synapsin-1 in co-cultured neurons, and decreased interleukin-17 A (IL-17 A) and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) activator 1 (ACT1) levels, suggesting involvement of IL-17 signaling. Knockdown of NOP58 in BV2 cells reduces neuroinflammation and synaptic damage in co-cultured neurons, highlighting its potential as a candidate therapeutic target in NMOSD.

title: C/EBPβ Drives Ischemia-Induced Microglial Inflammatory Reprogramming Through Transcriptional Activation of ATF3 and Exacerbates Brain Injury.
abstract: Microglial activation contributes substantially to secondary brain injury after ischemic stroke, but the transcriptional mechanisms governing this response remain poorly defined. Here, we identified CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein β (C/EBPβ) as a key regulator of ischemia-induced microglial inflammation. RNA sequencing of microglia isolated from mice subjected to transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) revealed extensive transcriptional reprogramming, characterized by activation of inflammatory pathways, including chemokine, TNF, IL-17, and efferocytosis signaling, as well as cell-cycle programs, together with suppression of homeostatic processes involved in synaptic regulation and neuronal support. Network analysis identified Cebpb as a highly connected hub across multiple inflammatory pathways. C/EBPβ expression was markedly increased in peri-infarct microglia after tMCAO and in primary microglia exposed to oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation. Microglia-selective Cebpb knockdown reduced TNF-α, IL-1β, CCL2, and CD16 expression, increased IL-4, IL-13, and ARG1 expression, and attenuated ischemia-induced morphological remodeling. Consistent effects were observed in primary microglia and BV2 cells, supporting a central role for C/EBPβ in microglial pro-inflammatory activation under ischemic conditions. Mechanistically, C/EBPβ directly bound the Atf3 promoter and activated its transcription, while ATF3 partially mediated C/EBPβ-dependent Il1b induction. In vivo, microglial Cebpb knockdown reduced acute ischemic lesion volume, neuronal apoptosis in the striatum and cortex, and long-term cerebral atrophy. These histopathological improvements were accompanied by sustained recovery of neurological function, somatosensory performance, motor coordination, recognition memory, and spatial learning and memory. Collectively, these findings establish the C/EBPβ-ATF3 axis as a transcriptional pathway that promotes microglial inflammation and secondary neuronal injury after cerebral ischemia. Targeting microglial C/EBPβ may therefore limit ischemic brain damage and improve long-term neurological recovery after stroke.

title: Programmable and selective silencing of oncogenic fusion transcripts by CRISPR-Cas13b via breakpoint sequence recognition.
abstract: Oncogenic gene fusions are key drivers of cancer, yet most remain undruggable by current therapies. Here, we establish CRISPR-PspCas13b as a personalizable platform for systematic silencing of various fusion transcripts. We reveal that recognition and cleavage of the breakpoint sequence by PspCas13b disrupt the fusion transcript, resulting in efficient protein depletion. PspCas13b cleavage produces aberrant, translation-incompetent target RNA species, a subset of which harbors internal deletions proximal to the cleavage site.
